title: Application Secrets and Configuration Patterns
description: Review common patterns for securely managing secrets and configuration in Azure applications.

data.text: As applications grow, managing configuration becomes harder. Several patterns help keep secrets safe and configuration maintainable across development, staging, and production.

data.title: Patterns to Know
items: Managed Identity + Key Vault — no secrets in code
App Configuration + Key Vault references — centralized settings
Environment variables for local dev — .env files ignored by git
User-assigned managed identity — shared identity across resources
GitHub Secrets + Azure login — CI/CD without long-lived credentials

data.title: Local Development with .env and DefaultAzureCredential
data.content: Use environment variables locally and managed identities in Azure.

data.title: GitHub Actions with Azure Login
data.content: Deploy from GitHub without storing long-lived secrets in your repo.
data.code:
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/login@v1
        with:
          creds: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CREDENTIALS }}
      - run: az webapp up --name myApp --resource-group myRG

data.caption: How configuration flows from vaults and App Configuration into your app.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    KV["Key Vault"] -->|"Secret references"| AC["App Configuration"]
    AC -->|"Settings + flags"| App["Application"]
    MI["Managed Identity"] -->|"Authenticates"| KV
    MI -->|"Authenticates"| AC

data.title: Never Commit Secrets
data.text: Always add .env, appsettings.Production.json with real values, and any file containing secrets to .gitignore. Scan your repository with tools like git-secrets or GitHub secret scanning.

A good configuration design has one code path across environments and a different credential source in each environment. The application asks a credential for a token; the credential resolves to the developer sign-in locally, a federated identity in CI, and a managed identity in Azure. Configuration values come from App Configuration, and secrets come from Key Vault through references. Nothing environment-specific is compiled into the app.

data.title: The canonical ASP.NET Core wiring
data.content: One Program.cs for every environment. The only difference is which credential DefaultAzureCredential resolves to.

data.title: Configuration anti-patterns
items: Secrets in appsettings.json, docker-compose files, or pipeline YAML that is committed to Git.
A different code path for production, such as an if (isProduction) branch that loads a secret file.
One identity with Owner on the subscription because it was easier than assigning three data-plane roles.
Copying the same secret into Key Vault, App Configuration, and a pipeline variable; now there are three values to rotate.
Assuming environment variables are secret. Anyone with access to the process, a crash dump, or a diagnostic log can read them.

data.title: DefaultAzureCredential order matters
data.text: EnvironmentCredential runs before the developer tools and managed identity. If a stale AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, and AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET are present in your shell or app settings, they win, and you may authenticate as the wrong identity. Clear them when debugging local sign-in issues.

data.title: What interviewers look for
data.text: Describe the target architecture in one breath: managed identity, App Configuration for settings and flags, Key Vault for secrets, federated credentials in CI, and no secrets in the repository or image. Then mention rotation and audit, because interviewers listen for operational maturity, not just the happy path.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: DefaultAzureCredential adapts to local dev, CI, and Azure automatically.
Combine Key Vault, App Configuration, and managed identities for defense in depth.
Never hardcode secrets or store them in source control.
data.takeaway: The best secret is the one you never have to store. Managed identities make that possible.
